article_title: Buyers and Tastemakers Are Saying Spring 2027 Trends Start in This City
sub_title: Straight from the Copenhagen International Fashion Fair, one editor breaks down the trends buyers are eyeing for spring/summer 2027.
article_content: Fashion's coolest trade show, the Copenhagen International Fashion Fair, has its finger on the pulse of what you'll see in stores come March and April 2027. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . Fashion month might technically begin in New York , but for the last few years, I've found myself getting my first real read on the season several weeks earlier—and several thousand miles away. Every August, Copenhagen International Fashion Fair, better known as CIFF , takes over Copenhagen's sprawling Bella Center, bringing buyers, designers, editors, and industry insiders together to see what's coming next. While the term "trade show" might conjure images of fluorescent lighting and endless rows of booths, CIFF is anything but. It's cool, sexy, and increasingly one of the most important stops on the global fashion calendar. In recent years, CIFF's influence has stretched well beyond Copenhagen. The organization has staged showrooms in Paris and Milan and partnered with international fashion organizations and events, including the Council of Fashion Designers of America and Paraiso Miami Swim Week , as part of a larger push to bring global brands into the Scandinavian market while giving Danish and Nordic designers a bigger platform abroad. The result feels less like a traditional trade fair and more like a meeting point for the people deciding what fashion will actually look like six months from now. I'm wearing a CIFF-inspired accessories trend I spotted while browsing the halls of the Bella Center during Copenhagen Fashion Week! That's precisely why I keep coming back. CIFF has drawn me to Copenhagen for the past few years, and I've come to think of it as the first stop on my womenswear calendar—a preview of the ideas, silhouettes, colors, and products that will inevitably resurface once the New York , London, Milan, and Paris shows roll around. In Copenhagen, however, there's another layer to the trend forecasting: money . Buyers are placing their first major orders of the season at CIFF, meaning you're not just seeing what has runway or social media appeal. You're seeing what stores are actually betting people will want to buy. That space between creativity and commerce is particularly visible among Copenhagen Fashion Week names like Gestuz , Herskind , and OpéraSport , whose runway ideas can be traced back to the racks at the Bella Center through a much more commercial lens. Between those shows and the 1000+ brands gathered at CIFF this season, I spent the week comparing notes with buyers, tastemakers, and fellow editors about what they were seeing and, crucially, what they were buying. Consider this your first look at the trends poised to define spring 2027. If there was one styling trick I saw almost everywhere in Copenhagen, it was a scarf tied around the head. Bandanas and headscarves appeared on the OpéraSport runway and throughout Copenhagen Fashion Week , but what made the trend feel particularly convincing was how many buyers and editors had already adopted it themselves. Consider it the latest extension of that distinctly Scandinavian approach to getting dressed: Start with relatively simple pieces, then add one slightly unexpected element—preferably in a great color or print—to make the entire thing feel more interesting. At CIFF, scarves offered an easy injection of color against otherwise neutral outfits, whether tied under the chin, wrapped closely around the hair, or worn casually as a bandana. Frog closures aren't exactly new to the fashion conversation, but Copenhagen made it clear that the detail isn't disappearing anytime soon. If anything, it's becoming more deeply embedded in the way designers are approaching everyday clothes. The decorative knotted fastening has been steadily gaining ground over the past few seasons, appearing on everything from jackets and cardigans to blouses and dresses, and at CIFF, the detail felt less like a novelty and more like a fully established style code. It's a lesson in thoughtfully designed minimalist dressing! Humble flip-flops have been inching their way into high-fashion territory for seasons now, but Copenhagen might have finally completed the transformation. Havaianas was practically unavoidable during fashion week—most notably thanks to its ultra-viral kitten-heel flip-flops—and that influence spilled directly into CIFF. The Brazilian brand has become an unlikely fixture of Scandinavian style , where its ultra-casual sandals are routinely paired with the polished, minimalist clothing Copenhagen does best. For spring 2027, however, buyers seem ready to take the idea one step further. Across the fair, thong sandals were getting an upgrade: slightly higher heels, sleeker shapes, and more refined finishes that make them feel less beach-bound and more appropriate with trousers, skirts, and dresses. Copenhagen has a way of making you reconsider colors you hadn't previously thought much about, and for spring 2027, that color is moss green. At Gestuz, the earthy shade appeared with the brand's signature cool, slightly undone sensibility, making a hue that could easily skew outdoorsy feel unexpectedly sleek. Elsewhere throughout the week and inside CIFF, similarly murky greens offered a compelling alternative to the burgundy, brown, and khaki palettes that have defined fashion's recent infatuation with sophisticated neutrals. The easiest way to make a very Scandinavian outfit feel considerably less basic next spring? Pin something enormous to it. At Herskind, exaggerated brooches punctuated the brand's otherwise streamlined looks, adding a decorative, eccentric element to clean tailoring and layered separates. It's a small styling move with an outsized effect that feels particularly relevant after seasons of fashion becoming increasingly interested in personalization. article_title: The Cult Ralph Lauren Jacket Every Insider Is Trying to Get Their Hands On
sub_title: This in-demand windbreaker from Polo Ralph Lauren has risen to become a key It item.
article_content: When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . There are certain fashion pieces that seem to materialize everywhere at once—on the shoulders of editors rushing between shows, in the wardrobes of the street style set, and on the Instagram feeds of the women who always appear to know what's coming next. This season, that piece is a decidedly unfussy one: Polo Ralph Lauren 's cotton windbreaker. Equal parts classic Americana and downtown cool, it has become a favorite among fashion insiders, and predictably, it's getting increasingly difficult to find. The appeal is easy to understand. With its relaxed proportions, utilitarian spirit, and instantly recognizable Polo branding, it has the rare ability to make even the most thrown-together outfit look intentional. The real fashion-insider tell, however, is the scarcity. The jacket has been perpetually sold out, with limited sizes still surfacing at select retailers. Although it is difficult to find the It item in stock, it just dropped in a fresh kelly green colorway. Bright without feeling overly precious, it taps into fashion's ongoing appetite for saturated color while retaining the easy attitude that made the jacket a cult item in the first place. Consider it a wardrobe find that doesn't scream "trend." It simply makes everyone who sees it ask where you got it. If you've been waiting for your sign to secure one, this may be it. From the brand's spring 2026 lookbook to the street style scene at Paris Fashion Week to social media feeds, Polo Ralph Lauren is a mainstay of the fashion set. article_content: When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . Wait a minute. Are naked shoes the new naked dress ? I've spent years covering the evolution of daringly sheer fashion moments on red carpets , so I'm not easily fazed by celebrities' out-there outfits. That said, Margaret Qualley 's newest appearance managed to stop me in my tracks because she's wearing the ever-so-controversial Chanel barefoot sandals that debuted on the runway at the French house's cruise 2027 show in Biarritz in late April. With just a small swath of leather covering her heels and two thin straps tied around her ankles, Qualley essentially went barefoot on the red carpet. I, for one, commend her bravery! article_title: It's Early, But It's Here: The Summer-to-Fall Capsule Wardrobe 2 Style Experts Swear By
sub_title: If you want to get your summer-to-fall wardrobe in order, follow the lead of style experts Mandy Lee and Erin Walsh and add these pieces to your rotation.
article_content: From statement earrings to straight-leg denim, these are the staples everyone should have in their transitional wardrobes. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . The period between the end of summer and the beginning of fall may be brief, but it still requires a thoughtful approach to style. One day might call for a minidress with elevated flip-flops , and the next could require a lightweight jacket , trousers, and closed-toe flats. Mastering transitional dressing is the key to navigating these changing temperatures seamlessly. After more than six years of working in fashion, I've learned the trick isn't necessarily having more clothes. It's knowing which pieces can carry you through the temperature shift, many of which you can borrow from your summer and fall wardrobes. To get a fresh perspective on what that looks like this season, I tapped two insiders: Mandy Lee , fashion and trend analyst and TJ Maxx and Marshalls trend expert, and Erin Walsh, celebrity stylist and TJ Maxx and Marshalls style expert. While I don't want to give away everything they shared just yet, one thing I will divulge is that you should prepare for one big shift—saying goodbye to quiet luxury and a minimalist way of dressing. "We are entering a more maximalist space," Lee tells Who What Wear. "[Fashion] has been leaning very simple and structured, and that's great. It has given people a big chance to find their basics and everyday items; however, now, we will see people really get in touch with their personal styles and add personality to their looks." This renewed emphasis on personal style will show up not just in silhouettes but also in color. Lee anticipates chartreuse, earthy green, and different tones of blue will be everywhere. "I would keep your eye on purple too," she says. Keep scrolling to discover more insights from Lee as well as Walsh and then shop our favorite fashion finds for the season ahead. What are the key pieces every fashion person should have in their summer-to-fall wardrobe? It depends on who you are, what you need in your life, what your days look like, and what roles you're playing. That said, I think you need a killer pair of jeans and a transitional jacket or sweater that starts injecting some of those warmer textures like wool and cashmere into your wardrobe. What are your favorite styling techniques for navigating the transitional season? I love adding a thin turtleneck under a shirt. I also love elevating basics with statement jewelry and belts. If I'm going to invest in something new for fall, I will look for new shoes that feel grounded, such as a chunky boot or loafer, or something fresh that will cinch the waist. How would you recommend transitioning summer dresses into a fall-ready wardrobe? I would throw an oversize denim jacket on top and style it with a slouchy sock and a chunky boot. What denim silhouettes and trends do you think are worth investing in this year? I love a high-waisted, structured trouser denim style—something that feels very '70s inspired. I also love a sleek pair of straight-leg, high-waisted jeans. However, for the weekends, if you want to feel very relaxed, a pair of baggy jeans is the way to go. What color trends are you excited about for fall? Mustard yellow, burgundy, deep teal, and olive. All the rust tones too. You've worked with TJ Maxx and Marshalls for quite some time now. What makes them great destinations for summer-to-fall shopping? The pieces you'll find are versatile and timeless. It's not like because it worked last season, it won't work next season. Also, you never have to compromise. You will always find options that are valuable, luxurious, and elevated without having to compromise your budget. "The quiet luxury trend was big for quite a while, and now, fashion seems to be leaning into something more fun, more statement-making, and more punchy. From a designer perspective, brands know they need basics and everyday pieces, but they also understand that standout, special pieces can be a huge incentive for consumers to come to their brand and shop. People want those items that make them feel a little more individual." "This trend is really all about juxtaposition. You might have a crisp, tailored top paired with something sportier and made from a softer material on the bottom and then finish the look with a fun sneaker—something that's part espadrille and part metallic sneaker. I think this is a really easy way to take that love of comfort and make it feel a little more polished and age-appropriate while still carrying that sporty sensibility into your career. This aesthetic has a lot of power when it comes to appealing to a younger generation because it feels comfortable, current, and still put-together." "This trend goes hand in hand with the maximalist aesthetic. From beaded bags to a menswear-inspired tie or even glass orchid earrings, these fun pieces will pull together any look. What's also cool about [shopping at TJ Maxx and Marshalls] is that inventory varies from location to location, so every shopping trip can feel a little like a treasure hunt. You might go in looking for one thing and discover a whimsical accessory or unexpected piece that completely changes your outfit. The options really feel endless." Nikki Chwatt is an associate fashion editor based in New York City. She joined Who What Wear in 2024 after writing fashion, beauty, and lifestyle content for WWD, Well+Good, Editorialist, and more. With a passion for personal style and the creativity that comes with it, one of Chwatt's goals is to help others understand that there is no such thing as a “good” or “bad” style; it’s just about putting an outfit together that makes you feel confident in yourself.

There's a reason Copenhagen was just named the world's happiest city, topping the 2026 Happy City Index. This was my first time experiencing it in summer—10/10, would recommend. Naturally, I did what any curious person does and typed "Why are people in Copenhagen so happy?" into Google. What I found kept coming back to one idea: empowerment. The city consistently gets credit for how much it lets people design their own lives, and there's a lovely line in an article about the topic from the Danish professor Christian Bjørnskov that says, "What is special about Danish society is that it allows people to choose the kind of life they want to live." That's why so many people look to Copenhagen for its street style and why I feel so drawn to it. It's a reflection of how people actually want to dress rather than how an algorithm told them to be cool or chic. They are the embodiment of taking up space. Their concept of hygge is one I relate to. I have a Substack blog called To Life, With Love , after all. Hygge is about enjoying the simple, good parts of life together with people you care about, and that's something I try to practise every day. It's no wonder the fashion reflects the way people live here. Every day, people get dressed with intention, with joy, and with love, and it shows in the street style. I stayed at Hotel Ottilia in the old Carlsberg brewery. Other than the fact that it didn't have air conditioning (a privilege I've come to learn is a luxury now that I live in the U.S.), it was a perfect base. It was a little far from the centre of town for an event like fashion week, but it was a 15-minute cycle, something I ended up doing almost every day. By the end, I think I was biking for several hours a day. The hotel bikes had only three gears, and after arriving to one too many things sweaty, I switched to a LimeBike. Here's everything I wore in Copenhagen. Morning: OpéraSport sheer dress, Good American jeans I went to the OpéraSport show and was given this look to wear. I loved wearing the sheer top over a pair of baggy jeans. (These are Good American.) My first instinct was to wear the dress on its own with a contrasting set underneath, but I opted for the jeans instead. It was my first day, and I wanted to suss out how dressed up everyone else was going before I committed. That's the thing about a piece like this, though: Knowing I can style it at least two ways is a reason I'll buy something, and bonus if you're trying to pack light. It's another outfit for your trip. Evening: Stella Nova dress, Nike Moon Shoes This dress was lovely. I rode my bike to the presentation and opted for Nike Moon Shoes instead of kitten heels . For evening, I think I'd have preferred the kitten heels, but the dress's open back won me over. Later: Dissh matching set This was one of my favourite outfits of the trip. It's a dress and a pair of pants, and in true Scandi style , I wore them together. The beauty of it is I could wear each separately for the rest of the trip too. That first day was very, very hot, and since I'd committed to biking everywhere, the loose fabrics went down a treat. It's much easier to cycle in pants than a dress, although I'll maintain that riding a bike in a dress is very chic. To the show: Saint Art pants, The Frankie Shop shirt, basic tank I knew I'd be getting out of this almost the second I arrived, so I wanted something comfortable I could sit around in and get my makeup done in while still looking effortlessly cool. I didn't realise how valuable my flip-flops would be here or how much everyone in Copenhagen wears them. It made my shoe packing very easy, and honestly, it'd make a great carry-on-only hack. On the Gestuz runway I wore a boss '80s-inspired suit down the runway for Gestuz. I love a blue-collared shirt with work-style pants, and the khaki-and-blue combination was really striking. To watch: By Malene Birger dress, The Frankie Shop shirt, AWD sunglasses, Polène bag I loved the colour of this dress; it really popped in golden hour, which is exactly when the show was. I added the Frankie Shop shirt as a layering piece, and the pop of blue from the sunglasses tied back to my shoes. But the bag was the star: a special-edition Polène Béri Lif. It's out of stock now, and I feel very lucky to own what I can only describe as a piece of art. Showroom appointments: Oasis tee, Shona Joy pants On my final day, I attended a couple of showroom appointments before my last show. I wore my fiancé's old Oasis tee over these Shona Joy pants, and it was a genuinely cool look—right up until I put a massive tear in them adjusting the seat of my LimeBike. I look defeated here. It was hot, my pants were ripped, and I was running late. Classic fashion story. On the Almada runway For Almada, I walked in a black dress and a silk cape that billowed behind me as I moved. I felt beautiful. The brand actually operated a see-now, buy-now model for its debut runway, so you can actually shop this look right now ! From what I saw on the runways and, honestly, even more on the streets, here's what's worth stealing. Flip-Flops Everyone wears flip-flops in Copenhagen—to shows, to dinner, on a bike. It made my packing easy (although you know I brought more shoes than days), and it's the ultimate carry-on-only hack, which I did not do this trip. To alternate between styles, opt for leather, maybe kitten heels, and then the classic Havaianas. Maybe even throw in a jelly pair. Balloon Pants I love balloon pants. They're so comfortable, and I think they look good on everyone. They're bike-friendly, too, which goes far in Copenhagen. Draped Silk and Chiffon Bias-cut silk and layers of chiffon are fabrics that catch the light and the wind. I even wore the trend on the runway for Almada. Just look at this detail from By Malene Birger. A Pop of Blue Blue was my little obsession this trip. Move over, red! A single hit of blue—on sunglasses, a bag, or shoes—running through an otherwise neutral or tonal outfit is the easiest way to incorporate it. Blue was everywhere, and it's so easy to make it yours rather than copy the algorithm. Taking Up Space No matter where you live, this one's the most important to remember. In Copenhagen, the fashion people were not afraid to wear silhouettes that didn't make them look smaller. They wanted to take up space, and they wanted to do it loudly. They were confidently themselves. It's not just a trend. It's an actual way to live, and we should all want to steal it! Copenhagen reminded me that getting dressed is supposed to be fun. Sure, Scandi minimalism was still alive and well, but getting dressed here felt intentional. It's a moment at the beginning of your day where you decide who you are and show it to the world. I think that's why the happiest city in the world also happens to have the best street style. When people are free to choose the life they want, they know who they are, and they dress like it. Once again, I'm bringing a little bit of Copenhagen home with me: the permission to take up space loudly, to wear the things that make me feel like me. You don't need to be in Copenhagen to do it; you just have to let yourself be free. If Copenhagen showed me one thing, it's that curves aren't going anywhere. Take up all the space you want! Copenhagen Fashion Week for the spring/summer 2027 season came and went in the blink of an eye. In case you missed it, some major highlights included Almada Label presenting its first runway show in a see-now-buy-now format, designer Hillary Taymour bringing her New York -based brand Collina Strada to the city for a waterfront debut, By Malene Birger back on the schedule, and new Danish names like Stem, Taus, and Solitude Studios joining the schedule. But once again, off the runway, the street style stole the show. For four straight days, Scandi girls and stylish visitors from around the world took over the city's streets, showing off their best looks. Many embraced elegant outfit formulas and standout fashion trends worth noting for the summer-to-fall transition . Still, what stood out most was the distinct individuality. Every attendee proved that true chicness lies in personal expression rather than following rigid fashion rules or what's considered "in"—and that a bit of rain can never dampen great style. Ahead, discover the five top street-style trends that are perfect for pre-fall. These pieces are guaranteed to make getting dressed come September much easier. Sorry, micro shorts, but long Bermuda styles are here to stay. During Copenhagen Fashion Week , many elegant dressers leaned into the shorts' sophisticated vibe, pairing them with classic button-down shirts and pumps. However, we also saw fashion people take inspiration from celebrities like Hailey Bieber and Margot Robbie, pairing them with loose long-sleeve shirts —another trend that isn't going anywhere. When searching for the perfect pair, you really can't go wrong: choose from relaxed pull-on silhouettes or classic tailored options, in fabrics ranging from breezy linen to structured wool. Shop the trend: Given that the main mode of transportation in Copenhagen is by bike, we were surprised to see many people wearing heels—from wedge flip-flops to high-vamp pumps . However, when it came to flats, there was one specific style that was everywhere—perforated ballet flats. What makes this shoe perfect for pre-fall is that it keeps the foot covered while allowing breathability thanks to the perforations throughout. Shop the trend: If there's one thing Scandi girls know how to wear, it's jeans. And while they're known for overly baggy styles—many of which veer into balloon- or barrel-leg silhouettes —right now they're embracing the most classic denim shape: relaxed straight-leg jeans . The clean-cut design is seasonless and adaptable, and, most importantly, effortlessly pairs with different shoes. Shop the trend: What makes Copenhagen Fashion Week street style stand out most is how attendees intentionally add personal touches to each outfit. This is why many of these looks are saved on Pinterest. This season, fashion insiders enhanced their outfits by tying scarves made of silk and lace, as well as sequined belts, around their waists. We also saw attendees cinching their waists with simple button-down shirts or sweaters, proving that you can use what you already have in your wardrobe and still get the look. Shop the trend: From black leather and dark-wash denim to bold satin, pencil skirts were everywhere—and it makes sense. This skirt trend is one you can count on for pre-fall, fall, and even winter. It was spotted on the runways for the fall/winter 2026 collections at designers like Marc Jacobs , Miu Miu , and N°21. While the fashion houses focused on pairing the skirts with coordinating collarless jackets and fitted blazers, those in Copenhagen proved they also look chic when dressed down with colored button-down shirts and cropped tees. article_title: Gen Z Is Saying These 2016 Brands Are Relevant Again

article_content: When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . If you were old enough in 2016 to have a Tumblr account, stream Lana Del Rey, ask for a Brandy Melville gift card on your birthday, or beg your parents for a Juicy Couture tracksuit come Christmastime, you might want to look away. Some of the fashion brands that defined the mid-2010s are having a very unexpected second act in 2026, and this time, a new generation is leading the charge. It's funny seeing many of the trendy It items that I tossed by 2020 at the helm of this resurgence, but here they are. Early on, 2026 was marked as the new 2016. People posted photo dumps using retro Instagram filters of the past, took pictures at the pink wall in L.A., and ordered colorful drinks, but we need to talk about the brands that are at the center of this cultural renaissance. Below, find the 2016 brands to be seen in while the iconic year is back around. Remember when a Triangl bikini was the unofficial uniform for every beach vacation in 2015 and 2016? I had to have one back then even though the shipping from Australia took weeks. The brand's colorful, sporty bikinis are popping back up in the fashion conversation, proving that the swimwear millennials thought they'd left behind might actually have another summer in it. Consider this your warning before your old vacation photos start feeling aspirational again. Brandy Melville defined a certain corner of teenage fashion in the mid-2010s, so seeing it resurface feels especially nostalgic. Gen Z 's affinity for the brand is less about re-creating the exact outfits of 2016 and more about tapping into its ultra-casual, off-duty aesthetic. The tiny tees, relaxed sweats, and effortless basics suddenly feel very of-the-moment. Before quiet luxury and minimalist basics took over, FreeCity was the label that made casual clothes feel like a fashion statement. Its graphic sweatshirts, oversize silhouettes, and distinctly L.A. aesthetic are getting a second look as fashion's pendulum swings back toward more expressive, nostalgic dressing. In other words, the sweatshirt you thought was permanently trapped in your 2010s wardrobe might be worth digging out. If there is one brand that instantly transports millennials back to 2016—or even further into the 2000s—it's Juicy Couture. The velour tracksuit has already gone through one major revival, but Gen Z's continued infatuation with nostalgic dressing has kept the brand firmly in the conversation. This time around, the Juicy look feels less like a costume and more like part of a broader appetite for Y2K and early-2010s fashion. Madhappy was everywhere in the late 2010s, especially among celebrities and the Instagram set, thanks to its colorful sweats and optimistic branding. Now, as Gen Z continues to embrace elevated loungewear and streetwear, the brand's signature pieces feel surprisingly relevant. The lesson? A good sweatshirt with a fun logo really can survive a few fashion cycles. P.E Nation's bold, sporty pieces were tailor-made for the athleisure boom of the mid-2010s, when leggings and sneakers were acceptable pretty much everywhere. Now that sporty dressing is having another major moment, the brand's color-blocking, technical fabrics, and retro-inspired silhouettes feel right on time. Gen Z is proving that athleisure may never actually go away. It just gets reinvented every few years. article_title: Buyers and Tastemakers Are Saying Spring 2027 Trends Start in This City
sub_title: Straight from the Copenhagen International Fashion Fair, one editor breaks down the trends buyers are eyeing for spring/summer 2027.
article_content: Fashion's coolest trade show, the Copenhagen International Fashion Fair, has its finger on the pulse of what you'll see in stores come March and April 2027. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . Fashion month might technically begin in New York , but for the last few years, I've found myself getting my first real read on the season several weeks earlier—and several thousand miles away. Every August, Copenhagen International Fashion Fair, better known as CIFF , takes over Copenhagen's sprawling Bella Center, bringing buyers, designers, editors, and industry insiders together to see what's coming next. While the term "trade show" might conjure images of fluorescent lighting and endless rows of booths, CIFF is anything but. It's cool, sexy, and increasingly one of the most important stops on the global fashion calendar. In recent years, CIFF's influence has stretched well beyond Copenhagen. The organization has staged showrooms in Paris and Milan and partnered with international fashion organizations and events, including the Council of Fashion Designers of America and Paraiso Miami Swim Week , as part of a larger push to bring global brands into the Scandinavian market while giving Danish and Nordic designers a bigger platform abroad. The result feels less like a traditional trade fair and more like a meeting point for the people deciding what fashion will actually look like six months from now. I'm wearing a CIFF-inspired accessories trend I spotted while browsing the halls of the Bella Center during Copenhagen Fashion Week! That's precisely why I keep coming back. CIFF has drawn me to Copenhagen for the past few years, and I've come to think of it as the first stop on my womenswear calendar—a preview of the ideas, silhouettes, colors, and products that will inevitably resurface once the New York , London, Milan, and Paris shows roll around. In Copenhagen, however, there's another layer to the trend forecasting: money . Buyers are placing their first major orders of the season at CIFF, meaning you're not just seeing what has runway or social media appeal. You're seeing what stores are actually betting people will want to buy. That space between creativity and commerce is particularly visible among Copenhagen Fashion Week names like Gestuz , Herskind , and OpéraSport , whose runway ideas can be traced back to the racks at the Bella Center through a much more commercial lens. Between those shows and the 1000+ brands gathered at CIFF this season, I spent the week comparing notes with buyers, tastemakers, and fellow editors about what they were seeing and, crucially, what they were buying. Consider this your first look at the trends poised to define spring 2027. If there was one styling trick I saw almost everywhere in Copenhagen, it was a scarf tied around the head. Bandanas and headscarves appeared on the OpéraSport runway and throughout Copenhagen Fashion Week , but what made the trend feel particularly convincing was how many buyers and editors had already adopted it themselves. Consider it the latest extension of that distinctly Scandinavian approach to getting dressed: Start with relatively simple pieces, then add one slightly unexpected element—preferably in a great color or print—to make the entire thing feel more interesting. At CIFF, scarves offered an easy injection of color against otherwise neutral outfits, whether tied under the chin, wrapped closely around the hair, or worn casually as a bandana. Frog closures aren't exactly new to the fashion conversation, but Copenhagen made it clear that the detail isn't disappearing anytime soon. If anything, it's becoming more deeply embedded in the way designers are approaching everyday clothes. The decorative knotted fastening has been steadily gaining ground over the past few seasons, appearing on everything from jackets and cardigans to blouses and dresses, and at CIFF, the detail felt less like a novelty and more like a fully established style code. It's a lesson in thoughtfully designed minimalist dressing! Humble flip-flops have been inching their way into high-fashion territory for seasons now, but Copenhagen might have finally completed the transformation. Havaianas was practically unavoidable during fashion week—most notably thanks to its ultra-viral kitten-heel flip-flops—and that influence spilled directly into CIFF. The Brazilian brand has become an unlikely fixture of Scandinavian style , where its ultra-casual sandals are routinely paired with the polished, minimalist clothing Copenhagen does best. For spring 2027, however, buyers seem ready to take the idea one step further. Across the fair, thong sandals were getting an upgrade: slightly higher heels, sleeker shapes, and more refined finishes that make them feel less beach-bound and more appropriate with trousers, skirts, and dresses. Copenhagen has a way of making you reconsider colors you hadn't previously thought much about, and for spring 2027, that color is moss green. At Gestuz, the earthy shade appeared with the brand's signature cool, slightly undone sensibility, making a hue that could easily skew outdoorsy feel unexpectedly sleek. Elsewhere throughout the week and inside CIFF, similarly murky greens offered a compelling alternative to the burgundy, brown, and khaki palettes that have defined fashion's recent infatuation with sophisticated neutrals. The easiest way to make a very Scandinavian outfit feel considerably less basic next spring? Pin something enormous to it. At Herskind, exaggerated brooches punctuated the brand's otherwise streamlined looks, adding a decorative, eccentric element to clean tailoring and layered separates. It's a small styling move with an outsized effect that feels particularly relevant after seasons of fashion becoming increasingly interested in personalization. article_title: If You're ITK, You're Already Shopping These 7 Fall Shoe Trends and Skipping These 7
sub_title: See which fall 2026 shoe trends are taking priority among fashion insiders and which shoe styles are not trending as much anymore.
article_content: When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . Many months ago, we made our predictions on the fall 2026 shoe trends that will become the most noteworthy. While our runway predictions are never far off, the first glimpses of fall fashion are beginning to take shape, which means it's time to revisit the footwear silhouettes to know. It may not technically be fall yet, but there are already several specific trends that are resonating in the designer collections and IRL, and it's time to report on them. Of course, because everything is cyclical, a number of styles are slowly starting to lose favor while these newer ones take center stage. It's not to say that you should go and remove them from your closet right this second, but fashion people who stay ahead of things are quietly skipping them when shopping for anything new right now. If you also want to know what the insider set is into and, consequently, not into going into next season, consider this your download on the status of cool footwear. Here, see which fall 2026 shoe trends are taking priority among the fashion set and which styles are simply not trending as much anymore. Heavy satin finishes are the first shoe trend I'm already seeing resonating in the wild from what came down the runways in the fall designer collections, and based on all the early popularity, I know it's set to be one of the major styles of the season. Whether that means a pair of pretty pumps, elevated flats, or even modern sneakers , seemingly every pair of cool fall shoes is getting the satin treatment. Yep, Western boots are back, but maybe not like you're thinking. Instead of on-the-nose cowboy motifs, designers are taking a more modern approach with boots that take classic Western details, like stacked heels and suede finishes, and reimagine them to be sleeker. In his debut Celine spring 2026 collection , Creative Director Michael Rider sent model after model down the runway wearing derby shoes . Not quite as formal as oxfords but more sophisticated than your average ballet flats, derby shoes are the surprising new style that's just right for a dose of everyday polish. With more brands getting in on the look, I only expect the trend to gain momentum this fall. Heavy embellishments were a key shoe trend on the fall/winter 2026 runways, where they appeared either with feathers and laces, like at Prada , or an abundance of beading, like at Tory Burch . These pairs are paving the way for the rise in beautiful and intricate embellishments that will come to define the prettiest evening-ready shoes of fall and winter. I have nothing against croc embossing. It's still quite chic, but there's an obvious successor taking its place going into next season, and it's none other than eel print. The finish is popping up all over, from The Row's viral eel-printed loafers to Reformation's beloved Inez Flats . Calling it now: Eel is set to be the new croc when it comes to luxe leather finishes. It might be time to set aside those chunky '90s runners, at least outside of the gym, because the new lifestyle sneaker silhouette of the moment has arrived in the form of ballet sneakers. Featuring slim soles, rounded toe shapes, and scrunched-ankle details, this is the trend behind the current It pairs, including Nike Moon Shoes. If I sound like a broken record about high-vamp pumps by now, it's only because the silhouette is climbing in the ranks. Come fall, they'll fully take over other trending heel styles like Mary Janes as the new go-to to pair with skirts and, later on in the season, tights . sub_title: Our editor highlights the top trends fashion people will be wearing this fall and where exactly you can shop them.
article_content: When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . Fall is right around the corner. While I love the multicolored leaves and pumpkin desserts, fall fashion is probably my favorite thing about the season. I look to the most stylish people to get inspiration for my looks, and there have been a handful of seriously cool emerging trends among the fashion set that I'm so excited to incorporate into various fall outfit ideas . Don't worry. I don't believe in gatekeeping, so I've detailed each up-and-coming fall 2026 fashion trend and exactly where to shop for pieces you'll love. Yes, you read that correctly. Not only are the most coveted fall fashion trends detailed below, but there are also editor-approved shopping picks from top retailers to help you tap into your inner fashion person. The following trends are included: mules , dramatic brooches, skullcaps , funnel-neck jackets , and animal-print accessories. Keep scrolling to find your new favorite wardrobe item. Mules aren't new, but there's no denying that the style is having a big resurgence for fall 2026. While more experimental styles like mule sneakers have gone viral, I am leaning into classic silhouettes with a twist that you'll never get tired of. It's been a few years since the fashion set started embracing gold and silver brooches to accent their outfits. However, brooches have become more dramatic. Think Carrie Bradshaw–like voluminous florals and fluffy feathers. The most stylish fashion people have been looking to inject a bit of whimsy into their outfits, and I'm loving it. Crochet caps are usually a summer staple, but the skullcap has the potential to be huge in the upcoming months. The fitted look is less about functionality and more about adding a bit of personality to your look. We will probably see tighter knitted styles that are like beanies popping off as temperatures cool. If you want to add a fun, modern spin to your fall outerwear, consider a chic funnel-neck jacket. This cool style has appeared on top retail sites in a range of fabrications and iterations. From windbreaker-inspired takes to leather and suede jackets, the funnel-neck style will definitely be a mainstay for fall and winter. There's something satisfying about adding an animal-print pop in the form of a cool accessory to my favorite looks. I love classic leopard, but zebra, tiger, giraffe, and cow prints definitely feel more current for fall 2026. If you're grabbing a handbag, on-trend shoes, or a scarf, this is your sign to get it in a cool animal print. article_content: When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . As a millennial, it's almost unnerving to see tweens and teens wearing the exact same trends I wore in the early 2000s . It's like looking in a time-traveling mirror every time I spot capri pants , low-rise jeans, butterfly clips, jelly shoes , and everything else I absolutely insisted my parents buy me from Limited Too. While there are certain trends I personally refuse to bring back—hello, trucker hats—I'm more than willing to accept other items into my grown-up life in 2026. Case in point: wedges . Not all wedges are created equal, however. The shoe trend can easily veer into outdated, cheesy territory, but that's certainly not the case with Reformation 's new versions. Ref has collaborated with influencer Enya Umanzor on a trio of gorgeous wedges I need ASAP. "Inspired by Enya’s playful interpretation of femininity, [the wedges are] silky, whimsical, and finished with embroidered swirls along the heel, hand-drawn by Enya herself," Reformation explains on its website. article_content: From statement earrings to straight-leg denim, these are the staples everyone should have in their transitional wardrobes. The period between the end of summer and the beginning of fall may be brief, but it still requires a thoughtful approach to style. One day might call for a minidress with elevated flip-flops , and the next could require a lightweight jacket , trousers, and closed-toe flats. Mastering transitional dressing is the key to navigating these changing temperatures seamlessly. After more than six years of working in fashion, I've learned the trick isn't necessarily having more clothes. It's knowing which pieces can carry you through the temperature shift, many of which you can borrow from your summer and fall wardrobes. To get a fresh perspective on what that looks like this season, I tapped two insiders: Mandy Lee , fashion and trend analyst and TJ Maxx and Marshalls trend expert, and Erin Walsh, celebrity stylist and TJ Maxx and Marshalls style expert. While I don't want to give away everything they shared just yet, one thing I will divulge is that you should prepare for one big shift—saying goodbye to quiet luxury and a minimalist way of dressing. "We are entering a more maximalist space," Lee tells Who What Wear. "[Fashion] has been leaning very simple and structured, and that's great. It has given people a big chance to find their basics and everyday items; however, now, we will see people really get in touch with their personal styles and add personality to their looks." This renewed emphasis on personal style will show up not just in silhouettes but also in color. Lee anticipates chartreuse, earthy green, and different tones of blue will be everywhere. "I would keep your eye on purple too," she says. Keep scrolling to discover more insights from Lee as well as Walsh and then shop our favorite fashion finds for the season ahead. What are the key pieces every fashion person should have in their summer-to-fall wardrobe? It depends on who you are, what you need in your life, what your days look like, and what roles you're playing. That said, I think you need a killer pair of jeans and a transitional jacket or sweater that starts injecting some of those warmer textures like wool and cashmere into your wardrobe. What are your favorite styling techniques for navigating the transitional season? I love adding a thin turtleneck under a shirt. I also love elevating basics with statement jewelry and belts. If I'm going to invest in something new for fall, I will look for new shoes that feel grounded, such as a chunky boot or loafer, or something fresh that will cinch the waist. How would you recommend transitioning summer dresses into a fall-ready wardrobe? I would throw an oversize denim jacket on top and style it with a slouchy sock and a chunky boot. What denim silhouettes and trends do you think are worth investing in this year? I love a high-waisted, structured trouser denim style—something that feels very '70s inspired. I also love a sleek pair of straight-leg, high-waisted jeans. However, for the weekends, if you want to feel very relaxed, a pair of baggy jeans is the way to go. What color trends are you excited about for fall? Mustard yellow, burgundy, deep teal, and olive. All the rust tones too. You've worked with TJ Maxx and Marshalls for quite some time now. What makes them great destinations for summer-to-fall shopping? The pieces you'll find are versatile and timeless. It's not like because it worked last season, it won't work next season. Also, you never have to compromise. You will always find options that are valuable, luxurious, and elevated without having to compromise your budget. "The quiet luxury trend was big for quite a while, and now, fashion seems to be leaning into something more fun, more statement-making, and more punchy. From a designer perspective, brands know they need basics and everyday pieces, but they also understand that standout, special pieces can be a huge incentive for consumers to come to their brand and shop. People want those items that make them feel a little more individual." "This trend is really all about juxtaposition. You might have a crisp, tailored top paired with something sportier and made from a softer material on the bottom and then finish the look with a fun sneaker—something that's part espadrille and part metallic sneaker. I think this is a really easy way to take that love of comfort and make it feel a little more polished and age-appropriate while still carrying that sporty sensibility into your career. This aesthetic has a lot of power when it comes to appealing to a younger generation because it feels comfortable, current, and still put-together." "This trend goes hand in hand with the maximalist aesthetic. From beaded bags to a menswear-inspired tie or even glass orchid earrings, these fun pieces will pull together any look. What's also cool about [shopping at TJ Maxx and Marshalls] is that inventory varies from location to location, so every shopping trip can feel a little like a treasure hunt. You might go in looking for one thing and discover a whimsical accessory or unexpected piece that completely changes your outfit. The options really feel endless." article_title: The Fashion Person's Guide to Getting Dressed for the US Open
sub_title: Celebrities, tastemakers, and fashion editors share their best outfit inspiration and the wardrobe formulas they swear by.
article_content: Celebrities, tastemakers, and fashion editors share their best outfit inspiration and the wardrobe formulas they swear by. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . Every year, it feels like the US Open just gets bigger and bigger, and we predict it will hit its peak in 2026. The US Open is one of those rare sporting events where what you wear, drink, and eat and even who you meet is as much a part of the experience as the actual sport itself. The best fashion brands, restaurants, and cocktail makers come together for this event that exudes culture year after year. With New York fashion insiders, celebrities, and tennis fans descending on Flushing Meadows, the stands have grown to have fashion week–level street style appeal. What exactly should you wear to the US Open? We're looking to the women with the best seats—and the best wardrobes—for inspiration. The ideal outfit is comfortable and practical yet makes a subtle statement, from polished tennis-inspired looks to elevated summer outfits that happen to work perfectly for a day of watching matches. Here's what to wear, according to celebrities, tastemakers, and fashion editors. If you're looking for inspiration before planning your US Open outfits, there's no better place to start than celebrities' closets. With the event having a step-and-repeat backdrop now, it's become quite the spectacle for seeing what celebrities are wearing to court these days. Here's what they wear to watch the game while having Honey Deuce on tap. A lot of celebrity outfits read as overly styled, but this look on Sarah Pidgeon feels unique to her. A bold striped shirt with a vintage-inspired belt feels like the perfect "hello" to fall. Ralph Lauren will always be a go-to for the tennis crowd, and a teddy sweater with classic whites is always ideal. Simone Ashley is the blueprint here. If you're tired of wearing the classics and want to switch things up, look to Rosalía. A silk gown with elevated and thought-provoking accessories is the perfect idea if you want to really go all out. Ellen Pompeo sported an outfit that will forever be classic in the tennis world. Any match you attend would be the perfect backdrop for a look like this. Just choose your best polo, a crisp pair of white pants, and loafers. For the fashion crowd, this event has become the perfect opportunity to put a distinctly New York spin on tennis style. From them, you can expect directional accessories, unexpected proportions, and pieces that feel fashion-forward enough for the city but still make sense for a day spent in the stands. Here's what they swear by for the US Open. "Matching separates are always an easy go-to for me, especially when I'm on the road. When you're bouncing between matches, events, and different venues, the last thing you want to worry about is overthinking your outfit. Matching sets make it super easy to look polished and put-together while still feeling effortless. They're also perfect for those really hot tennis days when you want something lightweight and comfortable without sacrificing style. I can keep the outfit simple and let a few key jewelry or footwear pieces do the work of instantly elevating the look." — Ayan Broomfield , founder of Ayan's Aces "My go-to outfit formula for attending the US Open is simple but distinct—a draped cotton poplin mini by Khaite, the Tatia, which reads like a sculptural T-shirt. Clean lines, comfortable, completely sophisticated. I pair it with oversize sunglasses, leather sandals on a slim prism kitten heel, an Elsa Peretti Bone Cuff, Gypset Hoops by Jessica McCormack, a Gaia Ensemble Ring by Sophie Bille Brahe, and a JPG Shoulder Birkin. [It's] a look that wins in and out of the stadium. The lived-in accessories and elegant silhouettes … make a white dress and sandals feel entirely its own. This is the kind of outfit that pays homage to the woman who knows who she is and honors it. Jackie Kennedy did this so well, and I'd like to think she'd be fan of this look today. The perfect mix of elegant and sporty while not giving up comfort." — Paloma Meehan, author of Paloma Bella "Still Here jeans or jorts and a vintage top. Trying to find New York–based brands is always fun, especially for the US Open. Comfort is key for this slam, and the best accessory is obviously a Honey Deuce." — Paige Paul, founder of Dairy Boy "I love to keep things classic with pops of color. I love a minidress or skirt with a cable-knit sweater over the shoulders or tied around the waist to break things up. It's hard not to mention Ralph Lauren when thinking about the US Open. We are in New York, after all, and they are the official outfitter of the tournament. Clean, simple lines with a little injection of personality through color or fabric!" — Laura Jung , author of Digestifs "I dress for the round—or, really, the seat—not the tournament. Early rounds are casual, so I'll add a sporty twist or work in the US Open cap and the tournament colors (navy and yellow) in a tasteful way. By the quarters and semis or any day I've got better seats, I dress up a bit more. I'll go for a top or jewelry that's interesting from behind because when you're close to the court, I think it's fun to dress for the eyes behind you. And I always bring a sweater. It gets chilly once the sun goes down, and it's a good accessory in the meantime, worn over the shoulders or tied at the waist." — Judy Kam , creator of @judyonthecourt "Even though we think of late August in New York as swamp-like, the US Open gets sneaky cold about halfway through, and you find yourself wishing you hadn't dressed for the heat. For night sessions, I think a well-designed jacket and simple slacks are all you need for a great outfit. This white sport jacket from Eaves or my rum-colored leather jacket from St. Agni are always on heavy rotation with black pants and heeled sandals." — Jessica Schiffer , author of Hard Court Who better to ask what to wear to the US Open than the fashion editors who spend their days thinking about clothes? The New York–based editors at Who What Wear are regular attendees to the matches. Season after season, we've learned what works and what doesn't, so you can trust our outfit formulas. "My perfect US Open outfit feels equal parts sophisticated, athletic, and personal. There should always be a tailored or structured piece (my looks in the past consisted of pleated linen dresses and structured bags) and a flowy element for breathability. It's summer in New York City, after all! Slim sneakers are practical and look super chic when paired with a breezy dress, though I also love the idea of thong heels or structured wedges paired with slouchy, low-rise trousers and a slim-fitting polo. I'll probably follow this formula this year. For a bit of personality, add some of your favorite accessories. Think acrylic bangles or a fun pair of sunglasses to make if feel like an outfit from your closet and not tennis cosplay. When all else fails, drape a thin sweater or rugby shirt over your shoulders. It works every time. (And buy a hat while you're there, and put it on with your outfit if it goes!)" — Alyssa Brascia , associate beauty editor "I don't know if you've heard, but it's hot in New York in August and September, so whenever the US Open rolls around, I like to stick with light colors. (They also feel very tennis to me—don't ask me to explain why.) Pants feel too constricting when you're standing and sitting, so I'll often opt for a skirt and sleeveless top or lightweight dress in white or ivory. Tip: Skip sleeves to give yourself a chance to get a tan in between matches. If you're going to be hot, you might as well, right? For night matches, I'll pack a lightweight cotton knit or sporty jacket to toss on when the sun goes down." — Eliza Huber, associate editorial director "First thing's first: I always wear sneakers to the US Open and to any tournament, for that matter. It's a bit of a hike from the train to the courts, so comfortable shoes are a must. An easy midi dress, like the one I'm wearing in this photo, is foolproof. I always make sure it's lightweight and breathable for hot, humid days and nights. For daytime matches, I never wear short hemlines because the plastic seats can get uncomfortably hot for bare legs. I also never ever go to a daytime match without a wide-brim hat, preferably one that ties under the chin in case it's windy. I'm a serious tennis fan, so I never want to be away from my seat for too long, which means I'm in the sun for hours and need protection. (FYI: Depending on how close your seat is to the court, you will not be allowed to come and go until changeovers, so you'll risk missing chunks of the match if you go to the concession stand and/or bathroom often.)" — Erin Fitzpatrick, associate director of fashion news "Since being outside in the heat for a long time is likely in the cards for a match day, I'd go with a breezy midi dress, which is easier to sit in than a short one. A linen, poplin, or silk one from Dôen, Posse, or Reformation with chic flats or sandals would be ideal, plus a baseball hat and sunglasses to block the inevitable UV rays." — Allyson Payer, senior fashion editor "Getting ready for US Open season is always something I really look forward to as summer starts to cool down. I find myself inspired by what players wear on the courts and add an elevated twist to that. This dress, for example, made me feel like I was in tennis whites, but the quality of the design felt worthy of holding a diamond tennis racket. Anytime I find an elegant take on tenniswear, I'm intrigued." — Sierra Mayhew, fashion editor "The US Open is one of those occasions where the classics always win. A crisp white shirt, white jeans, and leather flats never feel out of place." — Kristen Nichols, associate director of special projects "Over the past few years, the US Open has become more than just a tennis tournament. It's also turned into a fashion show with spectators showcasing their most stylish outfits—sometimes perhaps a bit too much for the occasion. I've been attending the event for about five years, always during the evening sessions, and I've stuck to the same outfit formula: white jeans, a white tank top, black ballet flats, and a sweater casually draped over my shoulders. It's polished, effortlessly chic, and, most importantly, comfortable so I can fully enjoy the matches." — Nikki Chwatt, associate fashion editor Sierra Mayhew is a fashion editor at Who What Wear, bringing a decade of industry experience to the editorial team. Since joining in 2021, she has made her mark by blending luxury and accessible fashion, decoding runway trends, and curating must-have shopping lists. Before joining Who What Wear, Sierra sharpened her skills at Harper's Bazaar and Elle, with bylines in Bazaar.com and collaborated with iconic brands such as Gucci and Ferragamo. A graduate of the University of Notre Dame, Sierra translates editorial expertise into viral social content , making fashion engaging for a new generation. Her unique perspective is rooted in her love for travel, music, and discovering the hidden gems that make New York City a constant source of inspiration.

article_title: Everything I Wore to Copenhagen Fashion Week as a Midsize Model
sub_title: I'm a model who just walked and watched Copenhagen Fashion Week. Here are the outfits I wore and the trends I'm bringing home.
article_content: I'm a model who just walked and watched Copenhagen Fashion Week. Here are the outfits I wore and the trends I'm bringing home. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . Jennifer Atilémile is the definition of a woman who does it all. A true multi-hyphenate, she is a model, writer, creative, activist, and intellectual. As an editor in residence, she gives us a behind-the-scenes look at the fashion industry. Jennifer Atilémile is the definition of a woman who does it all. A true multi-hyphenate, she is a model, writer, creative, activist, and intellectual. As an editor in residence, she gives us a behind-the-scenes look at the fashion industry. I love Denmark. Every time I go, I come home with a renewed appreciation for my own life and for the Danes themselves. There's a reason Copenhagen was just named the world's happiest city, topping the 2026 Happy City Index. This was my first time experiencing it in summer—10/10, would recommend. Naturally, I did what any curious person does and typed "Why are people in Copenhagen so happy?" into Google. What I found kept coming back to one idea: empowerment. The city consistently gets credit for how much it lets people design their own lives, and there's a lovely line in an article about the topic from the Danish professor Christian Bjørnskov that says, "What is special about Danish society is that it allows people to choose the kind of life they want to live." That's why so many people look to Copenhagen for its street style and why I feel so drawn to it. It's a reflection of how people actually want to dress rather than how an algorithm told them to be cool or chic. They are the embodiment of taking up space. Their concept of hygge is one I relate to. I have a Substack blog called To Life, With Love , after all. Hygge is about enjoying the simple, good parts of life together with people you care about, and that's something I try to practise every day. It's no wonder the fashion reflects the way people live here. Every day, people get dressed with intention, with joy, and with love, and it shows in the street style. I stayed at Hotel Ottilia in the old Carlsberg brewery. Other than the fact that it didn't have air conditioning (a privilege I've come to learn is a luxury now that I live in the U.S.), it was a perfect base. It was a little far from the centre of town for an event like fashion week, but it was a 15-minute cycle, something I ended up doing almost every day. By the end, I think I was biking for several hours a day. The hotel bikes had only three gears, and after arriving to one too many things sweaty, I switched to a LimeBike. Here's everything I wore in Copenhagen. Morning: OpéraSport sheer dress, Good American jeans I went to the OpéraSport show and was given this look to wear. I loved wearing the sheer top over a pair of baggy jeans. (These are Good American.) My first instinct was to wear the dress on its own with a contrasting set underneath, but I opted for the jeans instead. It was my first day, and I wanted to suss out how dressed up everyone else was going before I committed. That's the thing about a piece like this, though: Knowing I can style it at least two ways is a reason I'll buy something, and bonus if you're trying to pack light. It's another outfit for your trip. Evening: Stella Nova dress, Nike Moon Shoes This dress was lovely. I rode my bike to the presentation and opted for Nike Moon Shoes instead of kitten heels . For evening, I think I'd have preferred the kitten heels, but the dress's open back won me over. Later: Dissh matching set This was one of my favourite outfits of the trip. It's a dress and a pair of pants, and in true Scandi style , I wore them together. The beauty of it is I could wear each separately for the rest of the trip too. That first day was very, very hot, and since I'd committed to biking everywhere, the loose fabrics went down a treat. It's much easier to cycle in pants than a dress, although I'll maintain that riding a bike in a dress is very chic. To the show: Saint Art pants, The Frankie Shop shirt, basic tank I knew I'd be getting out of this almost the second I arrived, so I wanted something comfortable I could sit around in and get my makeup done in while still looking effortlessly cool. I didn't realise how valuable my flip-flops would be here or how much everyone in Copenhagen wears them. It made my shoe packing very easy, and honestly, it'd make a great carry-on-only hack. On the Gestuz runway I wore a boss '80s-inspired suit down the runway for Gestuz. I love a blue-collared shirt with work-style pants, and the khaki-and-blue combination was really striking. To watch: By Malene Birger dress, The Frankie Shop shirt, AWD sunglasses, Polène bag I loved the colour of this dress; it really popped in golden hour, which is exactly when the show was. I added the Frankie Shop shirt as a layering piece, and the pop of blue from the sunglasses tied back to my shoes. But the bag was the star: a special-edition Polène Béri Lif. It's out of stock now, and I feel very lucky to own what I can only describe as a piece of art. Showroom appointments: Oasis tee, Shona Joy pants On my final day, I attended a couple of showroom appointments before my last show. I wore my fiancé's old Oasis tee over these Shona Joy pants, and it was a genuinely cool look—right up until I put a massive tear in them adjusting the seat of my LimeBike. I look defeated here. It was hot, my pants were ripped, and I was running late. Classic fashion story. On the Almada runway For Almada, I walked in a black dress and a silk cape that billowed behind me as I moved. I felt beautiful. The brand actually operated a see-now, buy-now model for its debut runway, so you can actually shop this look right now ! From what I saw on the runways and, honestly, even more on the streets, here's what's worth stealing. Flip-Flops Everyone wears flip-flops in Copenhagen—to shows, to dinner, on a bike. It made my packing easy (although you know I brought more shoes than days), and it's the ultimate carry-on-only hack, which I did not do this trip. To alternate between styles, opt for leather, maybe kitten heels, and then the classic Havaianas. Maybe even throw in a jelly pair. Balloon Pants I love balloon pants. They're so comfortable, and I think they look good on everyone. They're bike-friendly, too, which goes far in Copenhagen. Draped Silk and Chiffon Bias-cut silk and layers of chiffon are fabrics that catch the light and the wind. I even wore the trend on the runway for Almada. Just look at this detail from By Malene Birger. A Pop of Blue Blue was my little obsession this trip. Move over, red! A single hit of blue—on sunglasses, a bag, or shoes—running through an otherwise neutral or tonal outfit is the easiest way to incorporate it. Blue was everywhere, and it's so easy to make it yours rather than copy the algorithm. Taking Up Space No matter where you live, this one's the most important to remember. In Copenhagen, the fashion people were not afraid to wear silhouettes that didn't make them look smaller. They wanted to take up space, and they wanted to do it loudly. They were confidently themselves. It's not just a trend. It's an actual way to live, and we should all want to steal it! Copenhagen reminded me that getting dressed is supposed to be fun. Sure, Scandi minimalism was still alive and well, but getting dressed here felt intentional. It's a moment at the beginning of your day where you decide who you are and show it to the world. I think that's why the happiest city in the world also happens to have the best street style. When people are free to choose the life they want, they know who they are, and they dress like it. Once again, I'm bringing a little bit of Copenhagen home with me: the permission to take up space loudly, to wear the things that make me feel like me. You don't need to be in Copenhagen to do it; you just have to let yourself be free. If Copenhagen showed me one thing, it's that curves aren't going anywhere. Take up all the space you want! Every season, it feels like there's a new ludicrously capacious tote for the fashion set to fall in love with. Don't get me wrong, I love a beautiful designer bag , and yes, The Row’s Margaux is still sitting pretty at the top of my wish list, but lately, the bag I can’t stop noticing in New York isn't particularly precious at all. It's colorful, slightly slouchy, covered in hand-painted initials, and being thrown over the shoulders of some of the coolest women around. Enter Alex Mill’s Perfect canvas totes. Available in Daily, Weekday, and Weekend sizes, the sturdy carryalls have quietly become an It-girl staple, spotted on everyone from Emma Chamberlain and Kaia Gerber to Gwyneth Paltrow . The real draw, though, is the personalization: Each can be finished with a colorful hand-painted monogram that makes an otherwise simple canvas bag feel entirely your own. If you’re familiar with Alex Mill, the rise of the cool girl tote probably tracks. The New York brand was founded by Alex Drexler in 2012 with the goal of perfecting those deceptively simple wardrobe staples you actually want to live in. Today, with former J.Crew and Madewell designer Somsack Sikhounmuong at the creative helm, that same slightly preppy, slightly downtown, I just threw this on sensibility runs through everything it makes—including its totes. Right now, it feels like fashion is craving exactly that kind of personality. After years of quiet luxury and anonymous, logo-free minimalism, getting dressed is feeling fun again. We’re tying scarves onto handbags, piling on charms, hunting down vintage keychains, and choosing pieces that look like they could only belong to us . A perfectly pristine bag is nice, but one painted with your initials, stuffed with your laptop and lip glosses, and a little beaten up from carrying it everywhere? Much, much cooler. article_title: Gen Z Is Saying These 2016 Brands Are Relevant Again
sub_title: Gen Z is giving these iconic 2016 fashion brands a surprising comeback in 2026, from Triangl and Brandy Melville to Juicy Couture.
article_content: When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . If you were old enough in 2016 to have a Tumblr account, stream Lana Del Rey, ask for a Brandy Melville gift card on your birthday, or beg your parents for a Juicy Couture tracksuit come Christmastime, you might want to look away. Some of the fashion brands that defined the mid-2010s are having a very unexpected second act in 2026, and this time, a new generation is leading the charge. It's funny seeing many of the trendy It items that I tossed by 2020 at the helm of this resurgence, but here they are. Early on, 2026 was marked as the new 2016. People posted photo dumps using retro Instagram filters of the past, took pictures at the pink wall in L.A., and ordered colorful drinks, but we need to talk about the brands that are at the center of this cultural renaissance. Below, find the 2016 brands to be seen in while the iconic year is back around. Remember when a Triangl bikini was the unofficial uniform for every beach vacation in 2015 and 2016? I had to have one back then even though the shipping from Australia took weeks. The brand's colorful, sporty bikinis are popping back up in the fashion conversation, proving that the swimwear millennials thought they'd left behind might actually have another summer in it. Consider this your warning before your old vacation photos start feeling aspirational again. Brandy Melville defined a certain corner of teenage fashion in the mid-2010s, so seeing it resurface feels especially nostalgic. Gen Z 's affinity for the brand is less about re-creating the exact outfits of 2016 and more about tapping into its ultra-casual, off-duty aesthetic. The tiny tees, relaxed sweats, and effortless basics suddenly feel very of-the-moment. Before quiet luxury and minimalist basics took over, FreeCity was the label that made casual clothes feel like a fashion statement. Its graphic sweatshirts, oversize silhouettes, and distinctly L.A. aesthetic are getting a second look as fashion's pendulum swings back toward more expressive, nostalgic dressing. In other words, the sweatshirt you thought was permanently trapped in your 2010s wardrobe might be worth digging out. If there is one brand that instantly transports millennials back to 2016—or even further into the 2000s—it's Juicy Couture. The velour tracksuit has already gone through one major revival, but Gen Z's continued infatuation with nostalgic dressing has kept the brand firmly in the conversation. This time around, the Juicy look feels less like a costume and more like part of a broader appetite for Y2K and early-2010s fashion. Madhappy was everywhere in the late 2010s, especially among celebrities and the Instagram set, thanks to its colorful sweats and optimistic branding. Now, as Gen Z continues to embrace elevated loungewear and streetwear, the brand's signature pieces feel surprisingly relevant. The lesson? A good sweatshirt with a fun logo really can survive a few fashion cycles. P.E Nation's bold, sporty pieces were tailor-made for the athleisure boom of the mid-2010s, when leggings and sneakers were acceptable pretty much everywhere. Now that sporty dressing is having another major moment, the brand's color-blocking, technical fabrics, and retro-inspired silhouettes feel right on time. Gen Z is proving that athleisure may never actually go away. It just gets reinvented every few years. article_title: The 5 Copenhagen Fashion Week Street Style Trends That Are Perfect for Pre-Fall Dressing

Copenhagen Fashion Week for the spring/summer 2027 season came and went in the blink of an eye. In case you missed it, some major highlights included Almada Label presenting its first runway show in a see-now-buy-now format, designer Hillary Taymour bringing her New York -based brand Collina Strada to the city for a waterfront debut, By Malene Birger back on the schedule, and new Danish names like Stem, Taus, and Solitude Studios joining the schedule. But once again, off the runway, the street style stole the show. For four straight days, Scandi girls and stylish visitors from around the world took over the city's streets, showing off their best looks. Many embraced elegant outfit formulas and standout fashion trends worth noting for the summer-to-fall transition . Still, what stood out most was the distinct individuality. Every attendee proved that true chicness lies in personal expression rather than following rigid fashion rules or what's considered "in"—and that a bit of rain can never dampen great style. Ahead, discover the five top street-style trends that are perfect for pre-fall. These pieces are guaranteed to make getting dressed come September much easier. Sorry, micro shorts, but long Bermuda styles are here to stay. During Copenhagen Fashion Week , many elegant dressers leaned into the shorts' sophisticated vibe, pairing them with classic button-down shirts and pumps. However, we also saw fashion people take inspiration from celebrities like Hailey Bieber and Margot Robbie, pairing them with loose long-sleeve shirts —another trend that isn't going anywhere. When searching for the perfect pair, you really can't go wrong: choose from relaxed pull-on silhouettes or classic tailored options, in fabrics ranging from breezy linen to structured wool. Shop the trend: Given that the main mode of transportation in Copenhagen is by bike, we were surprised to see many people wearing heels—from wedge flip-flops to high-vamp pumps . However, when it came to flats, there was one specific style that was everywhere—perforated ballet flats. What makes this shoe perfect for pre-fall is that it keeps the foot covered while allowing breathability thanks to the perforations throughout. Shop the trend: If there's one thing Scandi girls know how to wear, it's jeans. And while they're known for overly baggy styles—many of which veer into balloon- or barrel-leg silhouettes —right now they're embracing the most classic denim shape: relaxed straight-leg jeans . The clean-cut design is seasonless and adaptable, and, most importantly, effortlessly pairs with different shoes. Shop the trend: What makes Copenhagen Fashion Week street style stand out most is how attendees intentionally add personal touches to each outfit. This is why many of these looks are saved on Pinterest. This season, fashion insiders enhanced their outfits by tying scarves made of silk and lace, as well as sequined belts, around their waists. We also saw attendees cinching their waists with simple button-down shirts or sweaters, proving that you can use what you already have in your wardrobe and still get the look. Shop the trend: From black leather and dark-wash denim to bold satin, pencil skirts were everywhere—and it makes sense. This skirt trend is one you can count on for pre-fall, fall, and even winter. It was spotted on the runways for the fall/winter 2026 collections at designers like Marc Jacobs , Miu Miu , and N°21. While the fashion houses focused on pairing the skirts with coordinating collarless jackets and fitted blazers, those in Copenhagen proved they also look chic when dressed down with colored button-down shirts and cropped tees.
